oil.summary: Crude closed out Q2 with a brutal session and an even grimmer quarterly scorecard — Brent -24.91% and WTI -25.98% on the month, the steepest quarterly decline since 2020. Today's 1d losses of 2.19% and 1.84% respectively extend the bleeding. The dominant macro driver remains optimism around a Hormuz/Iran peace deal, which has repriced a substantial geopolitical risk premium out of the market. A contrarian note worth flagging: one analysis argues an Iranian supply crunch could paradoxically push prices below $40, not above it. Bullish offsets are limited: the EIA reported a 3.8 mb draw for the week ending June 26, and Ukrainian drone strikes on two Russian refineries prompted Putin to acknowledge domestic fuel problems. India set a record 5 mb/d import pace in June, absorbing Hormuz-disrupted flows. RBOB and heating oil outperformed crude on the week, up modestly.
drivers: Iran peace-deal optimism has stripped a large geopolitical premium from Brent and WTI, driving the steepest quarterly selloff since 2020
EIA reported a 3.8 mb crude inventory draw for the week ending June 26, providing limited near-term support
Ukrainian drone strikes hit two Russian refineries; Putin admitted fuel supply problems, but market impact muted relative to macro bearish sentiment

gas.summary: Henry Hub slipped 1.62% on the day to $3.221/MMBtu but remains marginally positive on the month (+1.35%), suggesting steady underlying demand. TTF shed 0.68% to €43.15/MWh but is up 5.56% on the week, reflecting lingering European supply anxiety even as LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz reportedly continued uninterrupted despite regional tensions. The EU's formal ruling-out of any Russian gas return reinforces the structural bid under European prices. On the demand side, the IEA flagged $50 billion in planned U.S. coal and gas power investment this year as electricity demand surges, underpinning longer-dated gas consumption. JERA's creation of a standalone LNG trading subsidiary signals Japanese buyers are institutionalising supply security. News flow for domestic U.S. gas fundamentals is thin today beyond the power-sector demand angle.
drivers: EU formally rules out a return of Russian gas, maintaining a structural floor under TTF despite the monthly pullback
LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz continued despite escalating Iran-related tensions, capping the upside spike risk
IEA estimates $50 billion in U.S. coal and gas power investment in 2026, supporting the medium-term demand outlook for natural gas

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged down 0.60% to $75.41, broadly range-bound on the month (+0.61%), as lower TTF gas prices reduce marginal fuel-switching incentives and keep near-term abatement pressure subdued. The key structural story is bifurcating demand: Germany reported a record 58% renewable share of electricity consumption in H1 2026, up from 55.8% a year earlier, pointing to accelerating displacement of carbon-intensive generation in Europe. Simultaneously, the IEA's $50 billion U.S. coal-and-gas power capex figure underscores that fossil-fuel power investment is surging where renewables capacity has yet to catch up with AI-driven load growth — a theme reinforced by a separate commentary on the electricity intensity of the AI infrastructure buildout. KKR and SK's launch of South Korea's largest renewable platform adds to the global capacity build narrative. European industry remains divided on the upcoming ETS overhaul, creating near-term policy uncertainty for carbon pricing.
drivers: Germany hit a record 58% renewable electricity share in H1 2026, structurally reducing carbon exposure in the EU power stack
IEA-cited $50 billion U.S. fossil power investment and AI-driven electricity demand growth highlight a global supply-demand tightness narrative that supports longer-term gas and carbon prices
EU ETS overhaul uncertainty is generating industry splits, introducing near-term headline risk for EUA price direction
